teaser: Seven tons of granite, a woman's face, a king's beard, and a body smashed on purpose.
review_notes:
Met data: granite, about 164 cm high and 343 cm long, weight over seven tons; reign of Hatshepsut about 1479 to 1458 BC.
One of at least six granite sphinxes from her temple at Deir el-Bahri; smashed under Thutmose III about twenty years after her death and dumped in a nearby quarry.
Recovered by the Metropolitan Museum's Egyptian Expedition in the 1920s (Herbert Winlock) and reassembled; came to New York in 1931 through the division of finds.
Aswan to Thebes given as roughly 200 km (125 miles).
The motive for the destruction (securing the succession rather than personal hatred) is the current scholarly view, not a certainty.
Chest inscription: faint incised signs are visible between the lappets and the paws in the photo. The lesson says they give her throne name, Maatkare, with 'beloved of Amun': please check against the Met's transcription.
The rows of small pits on the chest and shoulder are read as traces of the pounding technique; the dark streak through the proper left eye is read as a natural vein in the stone. Both from the image only.
The paler, smoother zones on the front of the base and on the forelegs are read as modern fills from the 1920s-30s reconstruction; please confirm which areas are restored and that the fills are tinted filler rather than stone.
The ridged band beside the hind paw is identified as the tail curled around the haunch.
No cobra (uraeus) is visible on the brow in this photo, so it is not mentioned.

lesson.text: This animal weighs more than seven tons, about as much as a full-grown elephant. It is carved from a single block of granite, 3.4 meters long (over 11 feet). And when archaeologists found it, it was in pieces at the bottom of a pit.

The face belongs to Hatshepsut, who ruled Egypt for about twenty years in the 1400s BC. She began as regent, governing in place of her young stepson. Within a few years she took the full title for herself: not queen, but king.

A sphinx is the king's head on a lion's body. It says that the ruler has a human mind and an animal's strength. Every pharaoh could be shown this way, so the form was ready-made. The question for her sculptors was what to put on the head.

lesson.title: A king's head
lesson.text: From the neck up, everything is official equipment.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Full cheeks, a straight nose, a small closed mouth with the corners barely lifted. It is a calm, ageless mask, the standard face of a pharaoh, with nothing to tell you the sitter is a woman.

spots.title: The eyes
spots.text: Each eye is outlined by a raised rim that runs on toward the ear, with a brow drawn above it the same way. It is eye paint, carved. The dark streak through one eye is a natural vein in the granite.

spots.title: The headcloth
spots.text: The cloth that flares out behind the ears and falls onto the chest in two flaps is the nemes, worn only by kings. Fine stripes are cut all over it, and the ear sits on top, uncovered.

spots.title: The beard
spots.text: A long, squared block juts forward from the chin and ends in a flat cut. It is the ceremonial false beard of kingship, the most surprising thing to find on her portrait.

lesson.text: The beard was not a disguise. Everyone at court knew who she was, and her inscriptions often keep feminine word endings. In Egypt the office of king had a fixed costume, and whoever held the office wore it in stone, beard included.
Male pharaohs did not grow these beards either. The royal beard was a false one, tied on for ceremonies. On some statues you can see the strap carved along the jaw.

The stone is granite from Aswan, quarried roughly 200 kilometers (125 miles) up the Nile and floated downstream. Granite is too hard for copper chisels. Sculptors pounded it into shape with balls of even harder stone, then ground it smooth with sand. That labor was the point: granite meant forever. And the labor left its fingerprints on the lion's skin.

lesson.title: The skin of the stone
lesson.text: Three places where you can read how the granite was worked.

spots.title: Rows of pits
spots.text: On the chest and shoulder the surface is covered with small pits in slanting rows. Each one is a blow. The body was bruised into shape, hit by hit, and never polished like the face.

spots.title: The toes
spots.text: Four rounded toes, separated by deep grooves, each one ground out with sand and patience. Fur is not attempted anywhere: this stone only allows big, simple forms.

spots.title: The name
spots.text: Between the flaps of the headcloth, faint scratched signs run down the chest. They are hieroglyphs naming the owner: Maatkare, her throne name, “beloved of Amun.” Granite takes only shallow writing.

lesson.text: That shallow line of signs mattered as much as the seven tons around it. For the Egyptians a statue without a name was nobody. The name made the stone a living stand-in for the king, able to receive offerings forever. Remove the name and the person was gone.

She had at least six of these made for her temple at Deir el-Bahri, a terraced building set against the cliffs across the river from Thebes. They lined the route of religious processions, guarding the way in pairs.

About twenty years after Hatshepsut died, her stepson and successor, Thutmose III, had her statues dragged out of the temple, broken up and thrown into a nearby quarry. Her name was chiseled off walls across Egypt.

The rubble lay buried for some 3,400 years. In the 1920s an expedition from the Metropolitan Museum dug out the quarry and found thousands of fragments. Sorting them was a giant jigsaw puzzle. This sphinx, pieced back together, came to New York in 1931. Some pieces were never found, and you can see where.

lesson.title: The jigsaw
lesson.text: The repair does not hide. Two places give it away.

spots.title: A patch in the base
spots.text: On the front of the base, a band of stone looks paler and smoother than the speckled granite on either side, with straight edges. It is a modern fill, closing a gap between ancient blocks.

spots.title: The forelegs
spots.text: Behind the toes, the leg turns whitish and blotchy for a stretch. Here too the restorers bridged a missing piece and tinted the filler to sit quietly next to the original.

lesson.text: Those fills are honest on purpose. From across the gallery the lion looks whole. From two steps away you can tell what the sculptors made and what the museum added. Nobody will mistake the 1930s for the 1400s BC.

And the lion did come back whole, down to the parts an Egyptian sculptor never forgot. The body is a real cat's body: chest swelling between the paws, hind leg folded tight against the flank. One piece of the animal is easy to miss from this side.
Every lion has a tail. Where did the sculptors put this one?

spots.title: The tail
spots.text: It curls forward around the haunch and lies flat beside the hind paw, a ridged band hugging the body. Nothing sticks out, so nothing could snap off. Even so, the statue did not escape the hammers.

lesson.text: Why did Thutmose wait twenty years to erase her? Historians now doubt it was hatred. He may have wanted the royal line to run cleanly from father to son, with no woman king in between. Whatever the reason, it failed. The quarry kept every piece, and her face is back on its lion.

quiz.question: What is a sphinx, in Egyptian art?
options: A bird with a human head
A lion's body with the king's head
quiz.explanation: It joins a human mind to a lion's strength.

quiz.question: Why does Hatshepsut wear a beard here?
options: It was part of the official costume of a king
The statue was recarved for a man
She wanted to hide that she was a woman
quiz.explanation: The false beard belonged to the office, and whoever was king wore it.

quiz.question: What happened to the sphinx about twenty years after her death?
options: It was smashed and dumped in a quarry
quiz.explanation: Thutmose III had her statues broken and thrown into a nearby quarry.

quiz.question: How was granite shaped?
options: Pounded with harder stones and ground with sand
quiz.explanation: Copper was too soft, so sculptors pounded and ground the stone.

quiz.question: Where did the sphinx originally stand?
options: At her temple at Deir el-Bahri
quiz.explanation: At least six of them lined the processional way of her temple.

quiz.question: What do the faint signs on the sphinx's chest record?
quiz.explanation: They are hieroglyphs giving her throne name, Maatkare.

facts.text: The sphinx was found intact, still standing at the temple.
facts.explanation: It was dug out of a quarry in fragments and pieced back together.

facts.text: Hatshepsut ruled Egypt with the title of king.
facts.explanation: She began as regent and then took the full title of king.

facts.text: The sphinx is made of soft limestone.
facts.explanation: It is carved from Aswan granite, one of the hardest stones the Egyptians used.
